This isn't strictly tech support as it doesn't involve a third party client but is silly enough to put here.

We have a large Oracle database full of customer information: names, addresses, dates of birth, etc. Normally the data come in automatically and we don't have to do anything. There is the occasional once-in-a-blue-moon incident where Oracle doesn't like the incoming data - recently a date of birth of 29th February 1985 came in and was changed to 1st January 1800 - but these are so rare we don't look for them.

Part 1: Starting summer 2015, $COLLEAGUE has had to enter some information manually. While I use SQLPlus in a Unix emulator, $COLLEAGUE prefers Microsoft Access to modify the database. He entered a string of dates of birth as DD-MM-YY, e.g. 09-04-77. Access displayed them afterwards as DD-MM-19YY, e.g. 09-04-1977, so he was happy.

Fast forward a few days.

By random chance (i.e. how I fix problems at work), I stumbled across some customers with dates of birth like DD-MM-00YY, who were therefore 19xx years old. $COLLEAGUE's name was next to the record so I spoke to him. We figured out that if you enter a date of birth as DD-MM-YY in Access, the Oracle database itself takes it as DD-MM-00YY but Access displays it as DD-MM-19YY. He swore that he saw it correct; I saw it incorrect. We were both telling the truth.

We corrected these and went on our merry ways, having learned a valuable lesson about Microsoft Access.

Part 2: A few weeks later, by the same random luck, I found a bunch of unclassified error codes. It turns out that a bunch of processes ran during the short period we had these very old customers in the database. In each instance, the age of the customer is calculated in years and months. The $YEARS field could only handle up to 3 digits, so someone 19xx years old broke the process.
Date handling, or our very old customers
It would be the stuff of nightmares if I were dealing with the problem remotely and we were seeing different things. Also, if I were dealing with someone non-tech savvy.
